newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aborigines mark civil rights anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Aborigines mark civil rights anniversary.

text.p: Aborigines on Tuesday celebrated the 30th anniversary of becoming Australian citizens with a "call to arms" against a current climate of racism and a demand for their rights to be enshrined in the nation's constitution.

"Today we are confronted with organised opposition based on race, based on skin and culture," said Faith Bandler, a South Sea Islander who 30 years ago led the push for Aboriginal and indigenous civil rights.

"In this climate of callousness, where a move to dismantle structures of democracy are heavily overshadowing us, our task now is to use our voices, our energy, our will...to mobilise the forces of good will," Bandler said.

"Our aspiration is to have the rights of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders recognised and enshrined in the Australian Constitution," Bandler told the Aboriginal Reconciliation Convention in Melbourne.
Unlike the U.S. constitution, the Australian constitution sets out predominately the role of government, not individual rights.
Bandler said the year 2001, the 100th anniversary of Australia's nationhood, will be the time to "stand and be counted" in the constitution.
On May 27, 1967, Australia passed a referendum granting Aborigines citizenship and the right to vote. Until then, Aborigines were governed nationally under flora and fauna laws.

But the celebrations on Tuesday were a mixture of hope and sadness -- hope that Australia was on the road to reconciliation between black and white, and sadness that Aborigines remained the most disadvantaged group in society.

The Aboriginal Reconciliation Council, which staged the convention, was established by government to produce a "national agreement of reconciliation" by the end of the century. Many Aborigines want a legal pact or treaty with white Australia.

Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Monday issued a personal apology for past ill-treatment of Aborigines, such as the abduction of tens of thousands of children under a policy of assimilation between the 1880s and the 1960s.

Australian Governor-General Sir William Deane, the representative of Britain's Queen Elizabeth, on Tuesday joined Howard, saying: "I want to say how profoundly sorry I personally am that things like that were ever done".
But many Aborigines argue their lives have improved little since 1967, and that many of their hard fought rights are now being eroded with a rise in racism and political indifference.
"Rights we fought so hard for are rapidly being eroded today," Aboriginal civil rights activist Rhoba Roberts told the National Press Club in Canberra.
Many Aborigines believe that if the 1967 referendum were held today it would be defeated. There are 300,000 Aborigines in Australia's 18 million population.
Howard's comment on Monday that Australian history since white settlement in 1788 was not a history of "imperialism and exploitation and racism" has drawn Aboriginal criticism.
Aborigines have also warned Howard that his plan to effectively extinguish native land title on farming land will ruin the reconciliation process.
"The government must have the courage to reset its priorities because there has been a disregard for human rights," said Bandler.
Deane told the convention that the injustices that fuelled the 1967 Aboriginal civil rights movement remain today.
Aboriginal life expectancy is 15 to 20 years less than the rest of Australia. Only 33 percent of indigenous children finish school compared with a national average of 77 percent.
